summary: Adds message relay intermediaries to MSRP, which was originally designed for direct peer-to-peer exchanges. The document describes the extensions needed to use relays. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Instead of passing notes directly, you can pass them through a helper in the middle who delivers them.

questions: how do relays work with msrp
what is the use-path header in msrp
how do msrp relays avoid being open relays
subtitle: How MSRP chat and file sessions can pass through relay servers without turning those servers into open relays.

tldr.problem: MSRP was designed for two clients talking directly, but clients behind firewalls or under policy rules need intermediaries, and relays must not become open relays for spam or denial of service.
tldr.mechanism: A client opens a TLS connection to a relay, proves who it is with an AUTH request using HTTP Digest authentication, and gets back a secret msrps: URI. Relays forward messages only when the To-Path starts with a URI they handed out.
tldr.outcome: MSRP traffic can cross any number of relays, and relays can split or merge message chunks along the way. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has since been updated by RFC 7977, RFC 8553 and RFC 8996.

today: RFC 4976 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 7977, RFC 8553 and RFC 8996, so read it together with those updates. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why MSRP Needs Relays
sections.content:
RFC 4975 defines the Message Session Relay Protocol (MSRP), which carries a session of messages directly between two end systems. Messages can be arbitrarily large and always travel over reliable, congestion-safe transports. RFC 4976 adds relays: intermediaries that forward messages and delivery status, and may enforce policy.

The goals include keeping direct client-to-client operation, allowing any number of relays under different administrative control, letting each client choose which relays act for it, and preventing spam, open relays and Denial of Service amplification. Large messages should not cause head-of-line blocking, interrupted transfers should be resumable, and relays should be able to delete state after a short time.

Clients that can receive new TCP connections directly do not have to implement anything new to work with these relays.
sections.eli5: Normally two kids pass notes straight to each other. Sometimes a wall is in the way, so a helper in the middle carries the notes, and the rules make sure the helper is only used by the kids who asked.

sections.title: Clients, Relays, Chunks and Paths
sections.content:
An MSRP node is a host acting as a client or a relay. A client is the initial sender or final target of messages; a relay forwards messages and delivery status. A chunk is a portion of a complete message carried in one SEND request. A hop is delivery between adjacent nodes; end-to-end means from the initiating client to the final target.

Routing uses two headers. The To-Path lists the URIs still to be visited, with the next hop leftmost and the final target rightmost. The From-Path lists how to get back to the sender. Unlike the To and From headers in SIP, they do not swap between request and response. When a relay forwards a request, it removes its own URI from the To-Path and inserts it as the first URI of the From-Path.

A SEND is acknowledged hop by hop by default. All other requests are acknowledged end to end. REPORT requests are never acknowledged.
sections.eli5: Each helper crosses their own name off the list of stops and writes it on the return address, so the answer knows the way home.

sections.title: Getting Access: the AUTH Request
sections.content:
A client that wants a relay opens a TLS connection, checks that the name in the relay's certificate matches the relay it meant to reach, then sends an AUTH request. The relay answers the first attempt with 401 Unauthorized and a WWW-Authenticate challenge. The client retries with an Authorization header, using HTTP Digest authentication from RFC 2617. Basic authentication MUST NOT be used.

A successful 200 OK carries a Use-Path header with one or more msrps: URIs, plus an Expires header giving the lifetime in whole seconds. The client can ask for a lifetime with its own Expires; a relay may refuse with Min-Expires or Max-Expires in a 423 response. URIs in Use-Path MUST use a fully qualified domain name and an explicit port.

With several relays, the client does a normal AUTH with the first, then sends a second AUTH to the next relay routed through the first. Each relay authenticates the client, and the client authenticates the first relay. The URIs are secret tokens, so a URI SHOULD be used for only one session, and the client MUST NOT reuse the same URI for multiple sessions.
sections.eli5: You show your ID at the front desk and get a secret pass with a time limit. You only share the pass with the friend you are talking to, and you get a new one for each friend.

sections.title: Forwarding Messages and Reports
sections.content:
Before forwarding, a relay checks that the first URI in the To-Path is one it created and handed out, and that the request is coming from, or heading toward, the client that got that URI. It also builds a fresh transaction id, since ids may not conflict on one connection.

For a SEND with Failure-Report: yes, the relay MUST answer the previous hop immediately; a 200 only means the chunk was received, not that it was forwarded. It then starts a timer when the last byte goes to the next hop. If 30 seconds pass without a response, it MUST build a REPORT with status 408 and send it to the original sender.

A relay MAY split a chunk into smaller ones or combine chunks into one, but MUST NOT combine chunks with different Message-ID values, and it SHOULD update the Byte-Range header. Requests with unknown methods are forwarded as if they were REPORTs. Responses go back over existing connections; if the connection has closed, the response is silently discarded.
sections.eli5: A helper says thanks as soon as a note lands in their hand, then watches the next handoff. If nobody confirms in a short time, they tell the sender something went wrong.

sections.title: Connections and Finding Relays
sections.content:
Relays reuse existing connections first and may open new ones, typically to other relays. When a relay receives an incoming connection, it waits up to 30 seconds for an MSRP request and closes the connection if none arrives. Relays should keep connections open as long as possible, and may close one unused for more than one hour. Clients should keep a relay connection until no sessions have used it for a local period that defaults to 5 minutes for foreign relays and one hour for the client's own relays.

To find a relay, an AUTH request's URI is resolved as follows. With a domain name and an explicit port, look up an A or AAAA record and connect with TLS over TCP. With a domain name and no port, do a DNS SRV lookup for the _msrps service on _tcp, falling back to an address lookup and the default port 2855. AUTH requests MUST only be sent over TLS, so no _msrp service is defined. Relay farms are RECOMMENDED to have an SRV entry per member.
sections.eli5: Helpers keep their phone lines open for a while in case you call again, and there is a phone book that tells you where to find a helper.

sections.title: Security Model
sections.content:
TLS is mandatory for clients and relays to implement. A relay presents a certificate whose SubjectAltName dnsName must match the hostname in the URI. A cipher suite of TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA MUST be supported. Relay-to-relay connections MUST use mutual TLS, and client-to-relay AUTH traffic MUST use TLS. Clients authenticate to relays with Digest; relays authenticate to each other with mutual TLS.

The anti-abuse core is the token. A relay forwards only traffic going to or coming from the client that holds a valid URI, and the URI MUST contain at least 64 bits of cryptographically random material. A third party who learns a token can send to that client but cannot make the relay send anywhere else. A relay that gets a request with an invalid URI MUST discard it.

The RFC admits the limits: relays are trusted nodes, and nothing stops a relay on the path from forging, altering or copying messages. S/MIME encryption and signatures can limit the damage and make tampering detectable in some cases.
sections.eli5: The secret pass is hard to guess, and it only opens one door. Even if a stranger finds it, they can only send notes to the one friend who owns it.

sections.title: IANA Registrations and Example
sections.content:
The RFC registers one new method, AUTH, and seven header fields: Expires, Min-Expires, Max-Expires, Use-Path, WWW-Authenticate, Authorization and Authentication-Info. It also registers one new status code, 401, default phrase Unauthorized.

Its worked example shows an SDP offer and answer, as carried in SIP, where Bob uses a relay. Bob's path attribute lists his relay first and his own URI last, so a sender reaches the relay before Bob.
sections.eli5: The RFC adds one new word and a few new labels to the official list of things MSRP understands.

viz.caption: PATH HEADERS BEFORE AND AFTER RELAY B FORWARDS (RFC 4976)

data.title: Path headers at relay B
data.code:
Received by B:
To-Path:   msrps://B.example.com/bbb;tcp msrps://Bob.example.com/bob;tcp
From-Path: msrps://A.example.com/aaa;tcp msrps://Alice.example.com/alice;tcp

After B forwards:
To-Path:   msrps://Bob.example.com/bob;tcp
From-Path: msrps://B.example.com/bbb;tcp msrps://A.example.com/aaa;tcp msrps://Alice.example.com/alice;tcp
